sections.normalized_html: Find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = 2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For a function [MATH: f(t)] defined on [MATH: [0,\infty),] the Laplace transform of [MATH: f,] denoted [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] or [MATH: F(s),] is a function of the variable [MATH: s] defined as [MATH: F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t] provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function [MATH: f(t)=2,] we have

[MATH: F(s) = ∫_{0}^{∞}2e^{− st}dt.]

We calculate our integral as follows:

[MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}2e^{− st}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{− st}dt]

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether [MATH: s \neq 0] or [MATH: s = 0.]

  • If [MATH: s \neq 0,] we have [MATH: F(s)|= 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{− st}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)(− (1)/(s)e^{− st})|_{0}^{a}; = − (2)/(s)(lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} − 1).] Let's evaluate the limit. We have [MATH: lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} = {0,|s > 0,; ∞,|s < 0.]

  • If [MATH: s = 0,] we have [MATH: F(0)|= 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{− 0t}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)t|_{0}^{a}; = 2lim_(a → ∞)(a − 0); = 2lim_(a → ∞)a; = ∞.]

Therefore:

  • For [MATH: s = 0,] we have that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t] is divergent

  • For [MATH: s > 0,] we have that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t] is convergent

  • For [MATH: s < 0,] we have that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t] is divergent

Evaluating our integral for [MATH: s > 0,] we have

[MATH: F(s)|= − (2)/(s)(lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} − 1); = − (2)/(s)(0 − 1); = (2)/(s).]

So, the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)=2] is [MATH: F(s) =\dfrac{2}{s},] defined for [MATH: s > 0.]

For the function [MATH: f(t)=e^{-2t},] we have [MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st} ⋅ e^{− 2t}dt; = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st − 2t}dt; = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt.]

We calculate our integral as follows: [MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt]

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether [MATH: s \neq -2] or [MATH: s = -2.]

  • If [MATH: s \neq -2,] we have [MATH: F(s)|= lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)((1)/(− 2 − s)e^{(− 2 − s)t})|_{0}^{a}; = (1)/(− 2 − s)(lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a} − 1); = (1)/(s + 2)(1 − lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a}); = (1)/(s + 2) − (1)/(s + 2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a}] Let's evaluate the limit. We have [MATH: lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a} = {0,|s > − 2,; ∞,|s < − 2.]

  • If [MATH: s = -2,] we have [MATH: F(− 2)|= lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{(− 2 − (− 2))t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{0t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)t|_{0}^{a}; = lim_(a → ∞)(a − 0); = lim_(a → ∞)a; = ∞.]

Therefore:

  • For [MATH: s \leq -2] the integral is divergent.

  • For [MATH: s > -2] the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for [MATH: s > -2,] we have

[MATH: F(s)|= (1)/(s + 2) − (1)/(s + 2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a}; = (1)/(s + 2) − (1)/(s + 2) ⋅ 0; = (1)/(s + 2).]

So the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)=e^{-2t}] is [MATH: F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s+2},] defined for [MATH: s > -2.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The Laplace transform of the function [MATH: f(t),] denoted [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\},] takes a function of [MATH: t] and transforms it into a new function of [MATH: s] as follows:
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s) = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-st} f(t)\,\textrm d t,]
provided that the improper integral is finite.

Content:
To build intuition, focus on the factor [MATH: e^{-st}.] For [MATH: s>0,] this factor decays to [MATH: 0] as [MATH: t\to\infty,] so it “discounts” the contribution of [MATH: f(t)] at large values of [MATH: t.]

Content:
This means the Laplace transform behaves like a weighted average of the values of [MATH: f(t)] on [MATH: [0,\infty),] where values of [MATH: f(t)] near [MATH: t=0] are counted more heavily than values far in the future.

Content:
Also, notice how the parameter [MATH: s] affects the discounting:

Content:
- If [MATH: s] is larger, then [MATH: e^{-st}] decays faster, so [MATH: F(s)] depends mostly on the behavior of [MATH: f(t)] near [MATH: t=0.]
- If [MATH: s] is smaller (but still positive), then [MATH: e^{-st}] decays more slowly, so values of [MATH: f(t)] for larger [MATH: t] have a larger influence on [MATH: F(s).]

Content:
Laplace transforms are especially useful in differential equations because they convert derivatives into algebraic expressions, which often makes it much easier to solve an initial value problem.

Content:
Note. When dealing with Laplace transforms, we're only interested in functions defined on [MATH: t \ge 0.] So for all functions [MATH: f(t), g(t),] etc., we will assume [MATH: t \ge 0] even when it is not stated explicitly.

Content:
Let's begin by calculating the Laplace transform of a constant function.

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating Laplace Transforms of Constant Functions

Example Prompt:
Find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = 2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For a function [MATH: f(t)] defined on [MATH: [0,\infty),] the Laplace transform of [MATH: f,] denoted [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] or [MATH: F(s),] is a function of the variable [MATH: s] defined as
[MATH: F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t]
provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function [MATH: f(t)=2,] we have

[MATH: F(s) = ∫_{0}^{∞}2e^{− st}dt.]

We calculate our integral as follows:

[MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}2e^{− st}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{− st}dt]

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether [MATH: s \neq 0] or [MATH: s = 0.]

- If [MATH: s \neq 0,] we have
[MATH: F(s)|= 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{− st}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)(− (1)/(s)e^{− st})|_{0}^{a}; = − (2)/(s)(lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} − 1).]
Let's evaluate the limit. We have
[MATH: lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} = {0,|s > 0,; ∞,|s < 0.]
- If [MATH: s = 0,] we have
[MATH: F(0)|= 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{− 0t}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}dt; = 2lim_(a → ∞)t|_{0}^{a}; = 2lim_(a → ∞)(a − 0); = 2lim_(a → ∞)a; = ∞.]

Therefore:

- For [MATH: s = 0,] we have that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t] is divergent
- For [MATH: s > 0,] we have that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t] is convergent
- For [MATH: s < 0,] we have that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t] is divergent

Evaluating our integral for [MATH: s > 0,] we have

[MATH: F(s)|= − (2)/(s)(lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} − 1); = − (2)/(s)(0 − 1); = (2)/(s).]

So, the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)=2] is [MATH: F(s) =\dfrac{2}{s},] defined for [MATH: s > 0.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Laplace Transforms of Exponential Functions

Content:
Exponential functions appear frequently in differential equations, especially when modeling growth, decay, or oscillations. Because of this, being able to compute the Laplace transform of an exponential function is a key skill that we will use many times throughout this course.

Content:
Suppose we want to find the Laplace transform of an exponential function
[MATH: f(t)=e^{kt},]
where [MATH: k] is a real constant.

Content:
We start from the definition:
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\}=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-st}e^{kt}\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
Next, we combine the exponentials:
[MATH: e^{-st}e^{kt}=e^{-(s-k)t},]
so the Laplace transform becomes
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\}=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(s-k)t}\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
From here, we evaluate this improper integral by writing it as a limit,
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(s-k)t}\,\textrm d t
=
\lim_{a\to\infty}\int_{0}^{a} e^{-(s-k)t}\,\textrm d t,]
and then checking which values of [MATH: s] make the limit finite.

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: When Does a Laplace Transform Converge?

Content:
Many Laplace transforms in this lesson reduce to an integral of the form
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{(a-s)t}\,\textrm d t,]
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: s] are real numbers.

Content:
To decide whether this improper integral is finite, we look at the exponent [MATH: (a-s)t.]

Content:
- If [MATH: s>a,] then [MATH: a-s<0,] so [MATH: e^{(a-s)t}] decays to [MATH: 0] as [MATH: t\to\infty.]
In this case, the integral is convergent.
- If [MATH: s=a,] then [MATH: e^{(a-s)t}=e^{0t}=1,] so the integral becomes [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} 1\,\textrm d t,] which is divergent.
- If [MATH: s < a,] then [MATH: a-s>0,] so [MATH: e^{(a-s)t}] grows without bound as [MATH: t\to\infty,] and the integral is divergent.

Content:
So, a common rule of thumb is that [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{(a-s)t}\,\textrm d t] converges exactly when [MATH: s>a.]

Content:
We will use this idea repeatedly when finding Laplace transforms and determining which values of [MATH: s] make the transform exist.

Item 7 — Example: Evaluating Laplace Transforms of Real Exponential Functions

Example Prompt:
Find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{-2t}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For a function [MATH: f(t)] defined on [MATH: [0,\infty),] the Laplace transform of [MATH: f,] denoted [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] or [MATH: F(s),] is a function of the variable [MATH: s] defined as
[MATH: F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} =
\int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t]
provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function [MATH: f(t)=e^{-2t},] we have
[MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st} ⋅ e^{− 2t}dt; = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st − 2t}dt; = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt.]

We calculate our integral as follows:
[MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt]

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether [MATH: s \neq -2] or [MATH: s = -2.]

- If [MATH: s \neq -2,] we have
[MATH: F(s)|= lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{(− 2 − s)t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)((1)/(− 2 − s)e^{(− 2 − s)t})|_{0}^{a}; = (1)/(− 2 − s)(lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a} − 1); = (1)/(s + 2)(1 − lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a}); = (1)/(s + 2) − (1)/(s + 2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a}]
Let's evaluate the limit. We have
[MATH: lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a} = {0,|s > − 2,; ∞,|s < − 2.]
- If [MATH: s = -2,] we have
[MATH: F(− 2)|= lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{(− 2 − (− 2))t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{0t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)t|_{0}^{a}; = lim_(a → ∞)(a − 0); = lim_(a → ∞)a; = ∞.]

Therefore:

- For [MATH: s \leq -2] the integral is divergent.
- For [MATH: s > -2] the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for [MATH: s > -2,] we have

[MATH: F(s)|= (1)/(s + 2) − (1)/(s + 2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)e^{(− 2 − s)a}; = (1)/(s + 2) − (1)/(s + 2) ⋅ 0; = (1)/(s + 2).]

So the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)=e^{-2t}] is [MATH: F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s+2},] defined for [MATH: s > -2.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Laplace Transforms as Functions of a Complex Variable

Content:
So far, we have considered Laplace transforms of real-valued functions [MATH: f(t).] However, the definition still makes sense for complex-valued functions.

Content:
If [MATH: f(t)] is complex-valued, we can write
[MATH: f(t)=u(t)+\mathrm{i} v(t),]
where [MATH: u(t)] and [MATH: v(t)] are real-valued functions.

Content:
Then, the Laplace transform is defined by the same integral:
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{f(t)\right\}=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-st}f(t)\,\mathrm{d} t,]
and the result [MATH: F(s)] may be a complex number.

Content:
In this lesson, we will keep [MATH: s] real. Even with [MATH: s\in\mathbb R,] it is possible for [MATH: \mathcal L\left\{f(t)\right\}] to be complex-valued.

Content:
For example, if [MATH: f(t)=e^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}] for a real constant [MATH: \omega,] then
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\right\}
=
\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-st}e^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\,\mathrm{d} t.]
We won't prove this rigorously, but it can be shown that the usual methods of integration apply to integrals like this.

Content:
In the next example, we will compute the Laplace transforms of complex exponential functions, such as this one.

Item 11 — Example: Evaluating Laplace Transforms of Complex Exponentials

Example Prompt:
What is the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{2\textrm i t},] where [MATH: t, s \in\mathbb R?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

[MATH: L{f(t)}|= F(s) = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st}f(t)dt]

For the function [MATH: f(t)=e^{2\textrm i t},] we have

[MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st}e^{2\textrm{i}t}dt = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{(2\textrm{i} − s)t}dt.]

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

[MATH: F(s)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{(2\textrm{i} − s)t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}e^{(2\textrm{i} − s)t}dt; = lim_(a → ∞)((1)/(2\textrm{i} − s)e^{(2\textrm{i} − s)t})|_{0}^{a}; = (1)/(2\textrm{i} − s)(lim_(a → ∞)e^{(2\textrm{i} − s)a} − 1); = (1)/(s − 2\textrm{i})(1 − lim_(a → ∞)e^{(2\textrm{i} − s)a}); = (1)/(s − 2\textrm{i}) − (1)/(s − 2\textrm{i})(lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} ⋅ e^{2\textrm{i}a}).]

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

[MATH: e^{\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm i \sin\theta]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: F(s)= \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i} - \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i}\left[\lim_{a\to \infty}e^{ -sa}\cdot \left(\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)\right) \right].]

Now, we have the following cases:

- For [MATH: s < 0,] the term [MATH: e^{-sa}] increases without bound while [MATH: \cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)] oscillates rapidly as [MATH: a\to\infty.] Therefore, the limit does not exist for [MATH: s < 0.]
- For [MATH: s = 0,] we have simply [MATH: \cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a),] which oscillates rapidly as [MATH: a\to\infty.] Therefore, the limit does not exist for [MATH: s = 0.]
- For [MATH: s > 0,] the term [MATH: e^{-sa}] decays to zero while [MATH: \cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)] oscillates rapidly as [MATH: a\to\infty.] Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for [MATH: s > 0,] we have

[MATH: F(s)|= (1)/(s − 2\textrm{i}) − (1)/(s − 2\textrm{i})[lim_(a → ∞)e^{− sa} ⋅ (\cos (2a) + \textrm{i}\sin (2a))]; = (1)/(s − 2\textrm{i}) − 0; = (1)/(s − 2\textrm{i}).]

So, the Laplace transform of [MATH: e^{2\textrm i t}] is [MATH: F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i},] defined for [MATH: s>0.]

Item 15 — Tutorial: Existence of Laplace Transforms

[MATH: |f(t)| \le Ke^{at}, \qquad t>T.]

Content:
Equivalently, [MATH: f(t)] is of exponential order [MATH: a] if
[MATH: f(t)=\mathcal O\left(e^{at}\right)\textrm{ as }t\to\infty.]

Content:
It can be shown that if [MATH: f(t)] is piecewise continuous on [MATH: [0,\infty)] and [MATH: f(t)] is of exponential order [MATH: a,] then the Laplace transform [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}] exists for all [MATH: s>a.]
